title: From Path-Aware to Application-Aware Source Routing using Traffic Classes
problem: Traffic engineering (TE) must make difficult decisions about capacity planning, flow allocation, and traffic splitting among paths to minimize congestion. Source routing enables fine-grained control but traditional approaches lack application-aware decision making.
motivation: Different applications have different latency sensitivity, throughput requirements, and tolerance for congestion. Application-aware traffic classification at the edge can enable source routing to make smarter allocation decisions aligned with workload needs.
method: The approach extends PolKA (source routing — a technique where the sending computer picks each packet's path through the network) by adding traffic classification at the network edge, the boundary where data enters the network. It develops traffic patterns and fair queuing methods to allocate network capacity fairly across different applications based on their type. The system uses in-band network telemetry (INT — measurement that happens inside the network as packets flow) and P4 programmable switches to identify what application each packet comes from and decide which path to send it on.
key_novelty: The core contribution is combining traffic classification at the network edge with source routing (path selection by the sending computer), so the network can allocate paths based on what application each packet belongs to rather than treating all traffic the same.
contributions: Traffic classification framework at network edge
Tailored queuing methods for fair allocation across traffic classes
Integration with source routing (PolKA) for application-aware decisions
In-band network telemetry (INT) and P4 programmable forwarding
Optimized network utilization and fair traffic class satisfaction
limitations: Abstract provides concept overview; specific evaluation metrics and workload characteristics not detailed.
